question.text: Academics from this country, the home of the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, fight "history wars" over the legacy of its colonization by the First Fleet.
question.clue: Governor William Bligh was deposed in the Rum Rebellion in this country.

swap.leadin: Descendents of convicts known as "currency lads" carried out raids on feral horses called brumbies in the bush and this region.
swap.text: Name this region where jackaroos established "cattle empires" around stations. The disastrous Emu War occurred in this rural region of central Australia.
swap.clue: An overland telegraph line through this region was scouted by Robert Burke and William Wills but was eventually built through Alice Springs.

question.text: This is the collective name given to Aboriginals who were taken from their families and forced to assimilate into white society. In 2008, Prime Minister Kevin Rudd formally apologized to this group.
question.clue: An official 2007 apology to these people and their descendants was made by then-Prime Minister Kevin Rudd.

swap.leadin: In order to pass otherwise deadlocked legislation, this party called its country's only-ever joint sitting of Parliament in 1974.
swap.text: Name this party. Australia's 1975 constitutional crisis was caused by John Kerr's dismissal of a Prime Minister of this party, Gough Whitlam, after the Liberal-National Coalition blocked supply to this left-wing party's government.
swap.clue: This political party passed important social reforms under leaders like Bob Hawke and Gough Whitlam.

question.leadin: Answer the following about the only successful armed uprising in Australian history.
question.text: Major George Johnston invaded Government House and placed Bligh under arrest in this capital city of New South Wales.
question.clue: This city is the largest to be served by the Snowy Mountains Hydroelectric Scheme, whose construction caused its country to ease pro-white immigration policies.

swap.leadin: British colonists under George Arthur and indigenous inhabitants of this island fought in the 1820s Black War.
swap.text: Name this island, which was first settled by people crossing the Bass Strait. Europeans originally called it Van Diemen's Land.
swap.clue: In 1996, Martin Bryant killed 35 people on this island.

question.leadin: Answer the following about a World War I battle.
question.text: This military group, composed of soldiers from two nations, landed at Gallipoli at its namesake cove, but was disbanded after the campaign's failure.
question.answer: Australian and New Zealand Army Corps
question.clue: Alexander Godley collaborated with William Birdwood to oversee its operations, which didn't formally cease until another branch of it disbanded after Villers-Bretonneux.

swap.text: Australian and New Zealander forces were joined in this unit. This unit notably fought in World War I and names the national day of remembrance in those two countries, celebrated on April 25.
swap.clue: Their most notable action is remembered in the song titled "And the Band Played" a certain nationalist folk tune, was supported by the French from Kum Kale, and was advocated by Winston Churchill.

question.leadin: Answer the following about the "White Australia" policy of discrimination.
question.text: This Australian prime minister began dismantling White Australia in 1966, a year before his mysterious disappearance during a swimming incident while in office.
question.clue: A king of this name served under George Maniakes in the Varangian Guard, but was later imprisoned for stealing imperial plunder.

swap.leadin: Following this event, Lachlan Macquarie was appointed governor of a certain colony.
swap.text: Name this rebellion, caused by James MacArthur's importation of the titular alcoholic drink.
swap.clue: George Johnston met up with John Macarthur, the wealthy merchant for whom the warrant had been issued, and together they raised an army to storm the Government House.

question.text: In 2017, Australian Aboriginals and Torres Strait Islanders held a convention at this rock formation in central Australia that is sacred to local tribes.
question.clue: A major event in the Aboriginal Rights Movement was the 1985 ceremony that returned ownership of this monolith to the Anangu. A 99-year lease on this enormous monolith has kept the Anangu from forbidding people to climb it.

swap.leadin: Identify some things about the geography of Australia.
swap.text: This tallest mountain in Australia takes its name from a similar peak in Poland, which is named after a Polish hero of the American Revolutionary War.

question.leadin: Windradyne led his Wiradjuri people in rebellion against the British in the Bathurst Wars.
question.text: Like others who are recognized on National Sorry Day, Windradyne was one of these people, some of which hopefully still follow the songlines that were left after the Dreamings.
question.clue: Many of these people were taken from their families and integrated into white culture, becoming the Stolen Generation.

swap.leadin: Two accounts by the sailor Watkin Tench are important sources for the early history of this colony, whose European settlers arrived on the First Fleet.
swap.text: Name this colony to which British, Irish, and African convicts were transported in order to populate the new city of Sydney.
swap.answerHtml: New South Wales [or NSW; accept Botany Bay; accept Port Jackson; prompt on Australia]
swap.clue: The Tenterfield Oration, calling for states to unify for purposes of defense, was given in this state, which was also the landing spot for Arthur Phillip and the First Fleet.

question.leadin: Answer the following about prime ministers of Australia.
question.text: This Australian prime minister used the slogan "All the way with LBJ" to increase Australian involvement in the Vietnam War, but he is most famous for disappearing at Cheviot Beach in 1967.
question.clue: This prime minister declared that he was "all the way with LBJ" in showing his country's support for the Vietnam War.

swap.text: Menzies built credit among the middle class by calling them by this name, which titles a notable 1942 speech he made emphasizing his connections to ordinary people.

question.leadin: A famous cartoon of this event depicts the Governor of the territory in which it took place cowering under his bed.
question.text: Name this uprising, led by George Macarthur. Macarthur was angered by, among other things, a lien against one of his ships for abetting an escaped convict and Major George Johnston.
question.clue: This rebellion took place after the arrest of John Macarthur, a lieutenant of the New South Wales Corp. It was named for the nickname of the New South Wales Corp, which had to do with a product the Corp traded.

swap.text: Lindqvist recounted the mistreatment of Aboriginal Australians in a 2007 book titled for this phrase. This two-word Latin phrase names a legal doctrine used to justify colonization that was rejected by the Mabo case.
swap.answerHtml: terra nullius [accept terrae nullius; accept Terra Nullius: A Journey Through No One’s Land]

question.text: Later, New Zealand and Australia laid out their post-WWII military and political goals in the Canberra Pact, signed by this Australian prime minister. Frank Forde finished this prime minister's term after his death in office.
question.clue: This prime minister of Australia during World War Two, a member of the Labour Party, defended the policy by declaring the country "the home of the British race" in a 1942 speech.

swap.leadin: Celebrate Australia Day by getting some points on this bonus. FTPE.
swap.text: Australia Day commemorates the day in 1788 when this group of eleven convict-laden ships under the command of Arthur Phillip landed to establish the first European colony on the continent.
swap.clue: This group that arrived in Botany Bay in 1787. This group carried nearly 600 convicts from Portsmouth, England in a 250-day journey.
